name: Daily Montanan
title: We trust juries … until we don’t
description: We’re hypocrites. We love juries. The foundation of our justice system. In Montana, we trust juries to decide guilt and innocence for roughly 1,500 different crimes. We trust juries to decide who wins and who loses for civil causes of action. We trust juries, until we don’t. We trust juries to consider DNA, bloodstain, and fingerprint evidence, […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images).We’re hypocrites.
We love juries. The foundation of our justice system.
In Montana, we trust juries to decide guilt and innocence for roughly 1,500 different crimes. We trust juries to decide who wins and who loses for civil causes of action.
We trust juries, until we don’t.
We trust juries to consider DNA, bloodstain, and fingerprint evidence, to determine the credibility of witnesses, to listen to experts, and to examine photos.
But, we do not trust juries to know that someone injured in a car accident was not wearing a seat belt.  That important little fact – is hidden from juries.  By law. Section 61-13-106, Montana Code Annotated (2025) mandates that evidence of seat belt use or nonuse is inadmissible in any civil case. Never.
We made wearing a seat belt and shoulder harness mandatory in 1987. It’s the law. Today, roughly 27% of Montanans don’t wear them.
We all know that seat belts save lives. We’ve seen the commercials. We’ve heard the stories. A seat belt saved my life. Yet, more than one-in-four people in Montana gamble that they aren’t going to be in an accident.
So, what happens when someone playing Montana seat belt roulette is injured in an accident?  They sue the driver who caused the accident. And, the jury will never know that the plaintiff wasn’t wearing a seat belt or that wearing a seat belt would have prevented or reduced their injuries.  It’s against the law.
I respect Montana’s libertarian streak, but we need to rethink this one.
Every driver has a duty to drive in a safe and prudent manner.  If they cause an accident, that is negligence and, if someone is injured, the injured person is entitled to compensation.  In ancient times, like around 1980, judges and legislators didn’t think juries should hear seat belt evidence because they might confuse “causation” with “damages.”  Honest.
Today juries hear complex cases involving scientific analysis. Multimillion-dollar product liability cases. Complex commercial disputes. Medical malpractice cases. Juries make tough and difficult evaluations regarding all kinds of evidence. Just not about seat belts.
That is a bridge too far.
By law, every passenger must be restrained by a seat belt. It’s the driver’s responsibility to make sure they do. But, if they don’t – it is not negligence under Montana law.  Even when the evidence is clear that they would not have been injured or their injuries would not have been as significant – if they had just complied with the law and buckled up.
So, when a driver and their passengers refuse to buckle up they break the law. But that is not negligence and you can’t tell the jury.
If you were the driver who caused the accident, how would you feel?  Yes, you ran a stop light, but hey – if she had been wearing a seat belt, she would not have been seriously injured. But the jury will never know. It’s the law.  It’s called a “gag order.”  And, you will be held responsible for every injury, even those that could have been prevented.
But, don’t people have a responsibility to obey the law and to take reasonable and appropriate steps to prevent and mitigate injuries?  Like wearing a seat belt?  Yes, they do.
This isn’t justice. It’s warped. It’s an antiquated social policy that has been cemented into our law. It’s time to change it.
Montana law is outdated.  Paternalistic. It undermines the system it is intended to protect.
The world has changed.  It’s not the 1980s anymore.  The people sitting on our juries today are pretty sophisticated. Remember Court TV, the OJ trial, “Judge Judy,” and Law and Order?  We have come a long way from Perry Mason, where three questions would compel a confession.
Juries today can understand seat belts. They can understand the difference between what caused an accident and the damages. The concepts of fault for the crash and responsibility for the injuries are not rocket science.
Montana should repeal its “gag rule” statute.  Evidence that someone was not wearing a seat belt should be admissible. The jury should hear all relevant evidence.  Lawyers can argue about it.  Judges can give the jury instructions about the differences between “causation” and “damages”.
Other states have done this.  The sky didn’t fall.
It isn’t fair to hide relevant evidence from the jury.  That unfairness breeds distrust, not just in our courts, but our democracy.
When someone causes an accident, the injured parties are entitled to compensation for their injuries – just not those injuries that would have been prevented if they had obeyed the law and buckled up.
Seat belts save lives.  Use them.  And, change the law.

name: WyoFile
title: ‘Canadian superwolf’? Nope. So then why are Yellowstone wolves 50% heavier than Great Lakes wolves?
description:
Canis lupus body size is dynamic and complex, and biologists aren’t in total agreement about why wolves are much larger in some regions than others.
The post ‘Canadian superwolf’? Nope. So then why are Yellowstone wolves 50% heavier than Great Lakes wolves? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming wolves are stout compared to some other Lower 48 subpopulations, and the reason why they tend to run hefty is complicated.  
In May, biologist Ken Mills published an annual report of Wyoming wolves that included an analysis of their weights in the southern Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. 
Crunching data from 196 wolves that were captured and slung from a scale over the last 15 years, the large carnivore biologist reported that the average wolf weighs 92 pounds. Males were roughly 10-15 pounds heavier than females, topping out at 154 pounds. 
The average Wyoming wolf is about the size of a Bernese mountain dog, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department biologist wrote. That’s a big wolf.
A breakdown of what wolves weigh in the area around Voyageurs National Park region in Minnesota shows that they’re significantly smaller. Wolves roaming the ecosystem near the Ontario border average 61-62 pounds, with males at 68 pounds and females at 55 pounds.
The size difference is stark enough that the largest animal the Voyageurs Wolf Project has ever handled, a 91-pound male, is a touch lighter than the average Wyoming wolf out on the landscape. Moreover, wolves roaming south and east of Yellowstone National Park are a full 50% heavier, on average, than wolves that dwell in Minnesota’s northwoods. 

Three-year-old male wolf 1526M weighed 99.5 pounds during a capture operation in February 2026. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)

It’s a large enough size gap that barroom and comment board banter about the mythical Canadian superwolf might come to mind for some readers. Ever since Canis lupus was reintroduced into the Rocky Mountains some 31 years ago, western residents who weren’t happy about the return of a long-absent species have peddled a theory that the Alberta and British Columbia wolves imported into Yellowstone and the central Idaho wilderness were a larger, invasive species that’s far different than those exterminated during the settlement era. 
Wolf experts say that’s simply not true. Then why the clear disparity between the size of a Wyoming wolf and a northern Minnesota wolf? WyoFile spoke to a handful of biologists and geneticists and discovered that there’s no single straightforward reason for the body-size gap. Factors that explain wolf size are complex and include their key prey species, adaptations to environmental conditions and the percentage of coyote genetics in the population. The degree north is another consideration: There’s a biological principle, Bergmann’s Rule, that holds that the colder the climate, the larger the mammal, even within the same species. 
“It’s probably a little of all of the above, the factors that drive body size,” Mills said. 
Below, wolf experts weigh in on some of the reasons why Rocky Mountain wolves are significantly larger than their upper Midwestern counterparts. There’s some disagreement about the underlying causes, and no clear consensus. 
It’s all about food
Tom Gable, longtime leader of the University of Minnesota’s Voyageurs Wolf Project, believes wolves are smaller in the ecosystem where he studies the species largely because of diet. 
“I think it all comes down to body size of prey,” Gable said. “Wolves in our system, and a lot of the Great Lakes region, are killing deer. And deer are considerably smaller than elk and moose.” 
Wolf O5E, a yearling, during a 2023 Voyageurs Wolf Project capture operation. (University of Minnesota) 
There’s a cost-benefit tradeoff to being large, Gable said. The larger the wolf’s body size, the more calories and food it will require to survive. 
“You don’t want to be any bigger than you need to be to kill your prey,” Gable said. “You don’t need to be 100 pounds to kill a whitetail deer, whereas that might be very advantageous when you’re killing elk or taking down a moose.” 
Research in Minnesota and in Yellowstone National Park supports the idea of a connection between body size and prey base. When pioneering wolf biologist Dave Mech analyzed the weight of wolves farther east in Minnesota’s arrowhead region, he found slightly larger animals, according to Gable. 
“They have wolves that prey a bit more heavily on moose,” he said. “Wolves in [Mech’s] study area are bigger than ours are, even though we’re like 80, 100 miles apart.” 
In Yellowstone, where wolves often prey on elk and even bison, researchers have also found that wolves benefit from being large. Nearly two decades ago, Utah State University professor Dan MacNulty studied this dynamic for his dissertation and found that larger wolves fared better overall when going after prey.
“What I found was that the effect of body mass on hunting success varied depending upon which stage of the hunt the wolf was in,” MacNulty said. “This all has to do with the effects of body mass on locomotion.” 
Wolf research in Yellowstone has produced incredible photographs, including this shot of a bison shielding her late-season calf. She successfully fended off wolves from the 14-member Prospect Peak Pack. (Yellowstone National Park)
MacNulty looked at three phases of wolves hunting elk: Giving chase to a herd, singling out an animal and then taking it down. Large wolves, he said, were slower and had no advantage at singling out elk, which requires speed — their body size even hurt their cause. 
“But when it comes time to grab ahold of the individual elk, being bigger is definitely better,” MacNulty said. “Across the different phases, there is a net benefit of being bigger when it comes to hunting success.” 
What about genetics? 
For retired Yellowstone Wolf Project leader Doug Smith, the first factor that came to mind explaining why wolves in the Northern Rockies are larger is historical intermixing between coyotes and Midwestern wolves.

Doug Smith is a retired senior biologist who led the Yellowstone Wolf Project for nearly three decades. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

“They are mostly wolf, but they’ve hybridized in the past,” Smith told WyoFile. “That’s kind of bringing their sizes down.” 
In modern times, the Voyageurs Wolf Project has not documented any coyote-wolf litters, Gable said. 
Historically, it’s a different story. Great Lakes wolves’ genetic ancestry is mixed, not unlike the mixed ancestry of Eastern coyotes, which one study showed have an average genetic fingerprint of 64% coyote, 13% gray wolf, 13% eastern wolf and 10% domestic dog.
Princeton University geneticist Bridgett vonHoldt said that her measurements have found 10-20% coyote genetic ancestry in Great Lakes wolves. But genes that she’s tested from Rocky Mountain wolves and those farther west have never shown the signatures of any coyote ancestry, she said. 
“That can really have a long-term influence on how those animals are shaped, and what their size is,” vonHoldt told WyoFile. 
Additionally, vonHoldt said, Great Lakes wolves have adapted to their modern environment and prey base. The combination, she said, helps explain the size difference, even though it’s the “same subspecies” as those in the mountain West. 
That subspecies is Canis lupus nubilus, or the Great Plains wolf. Although there were once roughly 30 subspecies of gray wolves recognized, in modern times the count is down to about five, vonHoldt said. Taxonomists currently recognize the Arctic wolf, Mexican gray wolf, Eastern wolf, Great Plains wolf (nubilus) and Canadian timber wolf (occidentalis).
All the lines are blurred by the fact that wolves disperse long distances and the different subspecies — and even coyotes — can breed with each other, vonHoldt said. There are even significant physiological and genetic differences within individual subspecies.

Wolf biologist Ken Mills uses a very-high-frequency receiver to attempt to pinpoint the locations of collared members of the Togwotee Pack in July 2023. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

“There’s also a large amount of variation just among gray wolves in the western part of North America,” vanHoldt said. 
Mills, the Wyoming Game and Fish biologist, sees differences in “ecotype”— wolves adaptation to climate and habitat — as a notable part of the body size equation. Before Wyoming wolves were wiped out in the settlement era, the state likely served as a “transition zone” between a “plains wolf ecotype” and a wolf ecotype better suited to the mountains, he wrote in his analysis. 
The mountain wolf “ecotype” persisted in the Canadian Rockies, and it was those animals that were naturally recolonizing the western United States before the 1995-96 reintroduction, which successfully facilitated their establishment. 
Bergmann’s Rule and other complexities
Another wrinkle in the wolf body-size equation is the age of the animal — and average age within a population. 
Wyoming wolves typically don’t reach their peak weight until they are about 5 years old, according to Mills’ analysis. Juvenile male wolves (9-12 months old) had an average weight of 80 pounds, but that increased to an average of 107 pounds for males a year or older. 
Where wolves are hunted, like in Wyoming, the average age tends to be lower (and thus wolves are smaller) than where hunting isn’t allowed, such as the Great Lakes or Yellowstone National Park. 
That’s a nuance that would help bridge, rather than widen, the body-size gap between Wyoming and Minnesota wolves. 
Male and female wolves put on weight until they reach 4 to 5 years old, then they either stabilize or gradually decline. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Mech, the Minnesota researcher who’s studied wolves for a half century, told WyoFile in an email that he’d be “very surprised” if wolves in the Yellowstone region are truly 50% heavier than those that dwell around Voyageurs National Park. Wyoming wolves were captured and weighed in the winter, he pointed out, whereas the Minnesota research specimens were trapped later in the year, at a time when they tend to be slimmer.   
Gable, at the Voyageurs Wolf Project, didn’t think that the seasonality of captures explained too much of the size differences. A majority of their research wolves are captured in May, when they “should be in really good body condition” coming out of winter, he said. The average weight in their records from spring and summer captures is also similar to that of wolves captured in February through April. 
Mech’s take is that latitude, and Bergmann’s Rule (the colder the climate, the larger the average individual), is the best explanation for why Wyoming’s wolves are heavier. 
“Of course, Wyoming wolves are those from Alberta and [British Columbia], which are larger than those from Minnesota,” Mech wrote. “I do think Bergmann’s Rule dominates, and I say that because the weight trend seems to apply in Eurasia as well, despite the wide variety of other conditions, including prey species across all of circumpolar wolf range.” 
U.S. Geological Survey biologist Dave Mech spent more than 20 summers studying Arctic wolves on Ellesmere Island, where they were unafraid of humans and could be observed at close range. (USGS)
Other biologists WyoFile interviewed perceived the influence of Bergmann’s Rule quite differently. 
“I would say Bergmann’s Rule does apply, but it’s not that significant,” said Smith, the retired Yellowstone Wolf Project leader. “The biggest wolves historically in North America were buffalo wolves. They’re gone, but they were in the middle of the continent eating bison.” 
Mills, the Game and Fish biologist, also sees Wyoming wolves’ far-north Canadian origins as being a small part of the body-size equation.
“I think that’s the simplest explanation, but it explains the least amount of the [size] variation,” Mills said. “Yeah, I think Bergmann’s Rule has an impact, but it’s not the be-all, end-all.”
The post ‘Canadian superwolf’? Nope. So then why are Yellowstone wolves 50% heavier than Great Lakes wolves? appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming GOP doesn’t respect voters’ fundamental right to select nominees
description:
Lawsuit against state shows that Republican Party executive officers want to be kingmakers, opines columnist Kerry Drake.
The post Wyoming GOP doesn’t respect voters’ fundamental right to select nominees appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The officers running the Wyoming Republican Party don’t really want primary elections. 
Their actions prove that. Last week, the party sued the state so it can implement a plan to effectively endorse candidates and finance them before the party’s primary election. A state law prevents the party from making such changes.

Opinion

The GOP’s elite, led by Chairman Bryan Miller, wants to tell the party’s rank-and-file members what values and beliefs a “real Republican” candidate must possess to have the sacred “R” by their name on the general election ballot.
That’s a scary proposition to many Wyoming voters, but it’s apparently what party leaders want the most. 
Toss a pebble into Wyoming’s rarified air, and if it hits a person in a crowd before it lands, the chances it will be a Republican are mighty high. (Please note: This is not true if you conduct this test in Albany or Teton counties. But if you do it in Niobrara County, it’s nearly impossible to have any other result.)
This month, registered Republicans in Wyoming outnumber Democrats 212,099 to 30,199. People look at the Democrats’ puny numbers, plus the party’s lack of candidates willing to throw their hats into the ring, thus making competitive races rare, and know the only way to have a say in primary elections is to register as a Republican.
While most parties welcome such advantages, executive officers who run the Grand Old Party in Wyoming know it comes with the risk that they can’t control who is on the ballot and who will win. That’s why when people turn on their TV and open their mailbox, they see commercials or flyers that brand opponents RINOs, a derogatory term that means “Republican in name only.”
The party’s leadership wants to effectively cull the herd, so folks who win office will think and vote like they do. If they want to have the GOP’s imprimatur and the money that follows, candidates need to follow orders.
This goes against the long-standing practices of both major parties, which have remained impartial about candidates before the primary election and let voters pick the party’s nominees. This is codified in a state law that prohibits political parties from financially backing one of their candidates over others before the primary election.
Republican officials are sick and tired of not being able to put the “right” members of their party in office so they can set the agenda for state elected officials, state lawmakers and Wyoming’s congressional delegation. The only way to legally do that is to end the prohibition on backing a candidate before the primary.
In its federal lawsuit, the Wyoming Republican Party is challenging the constitutionality of the state law. It maintains that political parties have the “absolute First Amendment right” to endorse one candidate over another.
The legal challenge is only being made against the ban on a party to finance campaigns before the primary, including spending money to print and distribute voter guides that provide information about how “aligned” candidates are with the GOP’s platform. These highly subjective voter guides would also be available online.
At their state convention in April, Republicans passed bylaws that established a framework to vet, endorse and financially back candidates running in the primary election. They pretended that their bylaws trump state laws.
But that simply isn’t the case, as the party learned last week when, before filing its federal lawsuit, a state district court ruled that the party must follow state law in elections for local party leadership.
The far-right GOP zealots who comprise the party’s leadership team have long maintained that the state has no say in the Republican organizational structure and internal business because it’s a private group. They believe they have a constitutional right to anoint whoever they want to represent the party, before the primary election, voters be damned.
I know it must break the hearts of the Republican Party’s officers to see a member of their own party think for themselves and vote for candidates who are against banning abortion, for Medicaid expansion, or myriad other issues. But that’s the election system we have in this country: People are allowed to vote for candidates who are independent thinkers and won’t toe the GOP line.
If it means electing candidates who others consider so-called RINOs, it’s not the end of the world for the party. Elected members who are most “aligned” with the party’s platform may simply have to work harder to persuade others in their caucus to agree with them. It’s called politics.
The Republicans dug their own hole when the party made its No. 1 priority banning “crossover voting,” so Democrats can’t switch parties after the candidate filing period opens.
The reason the law passed wasn’t secret; Republicans didn’t want Democrats to “steal” their primaries by supporting more moderate candidates. But because so few Democrats actually switched parties, it was statistically impossible for them to be the deciding factor in the contest that most upset conservative Republicans: the 2018 gubernatorial primary, when Mark Gordon defeated two far-right rivals and went on to win the general election.
But in races like the crowded 10-candidate field in the Republican U.S. House primary, temporarily converted Democrats, independents and RINOs can split the vote and accomplish exactly what the party feared. That means the most conservative, pliable candidate — the one most likely to peddle any red-meat cultural issue party leaders want pushed on a given day — may not get the nomination.
The Wyoming Republican Party can’t have it both ways. It can’t be a private club that ignores state laws and also benefits from a process in which the state and counties pay to administer elections. There’s no official figure on how much it costs to put on a statewide election, but the most recent estimate I’ve heard is about $1.2 million.
To my knowledge, no Republican official has ever said the party will pony up that much money to run its own primary election. If this private club isn’t willing to spend the party’s money to do so, it must either adhere to state election laws or pass legislation to change them. Winning this lawsuit won’t free the Republican Party from the debt it incurs operating its own primary.
A state law that prohibits a political party from financing one person’s candidacy over others wouldn’t be the subject of litigation if the GOP respected the fundamental rights of its own members. Voters who register with a party and obtain its ballot expect it to be neutral in primaries. Let the people, and not the party kingmakers, choose our leaders.

title: Will the Wyoming Freedom Caucus win control of the Senate? Here are the races to watch.
description:
Several caucus members and allies are leaving the House to pursue seats in the upper chamber. 
The post Will the Wyoming Freedom Caucus win control of the Senate? Here are the races to watch. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
While Wyoming’s top elected officials will be on the ballot this year, those aren’t the only races that will determine the direction of the state. Voters also will decide whether to give the Wyoming Freedom Caucus control of the Senate in the Wyoming Legislature. That possible shift in power will come down to several key races. 
The caucus, which bills itself as the genuine conservative voice of the Republican Party, aims to build on its victorious 2024 election season, when it won control of the House. Now, several caucus members and allies are leaving the House to pursue Senate seats, keeping with plans the group laid out following the 2026 budget session. 
After most of its top legislative goals failed this year, the caucus chalked its losses up to lacking a supermajority in the House and a lack of Freedom Caucus support in the Senate. 

State Superintendent candidate Rachel Rodriguez-Williams of Park County gives her speech during the Wyoming Republican State Convention on Saturday, April 25, 2026, in Douglas. (Dan Cepeda/WyoFile)

“Regardless of where our priorities failed, it’s clear that we need reinforcements in Cheyenne,” Rep. Rachel Rodriguez-Williams told reporters at a post-session press conference. Williams, who chairs the caucus, is now running for secretary of state. 
Unlike the House, where there’s a distinct division between caucus-aligned representatives and other members, the Senate is more heterogeneous. The upper chamber is a supermajority Republican body, but votes there are not always predictable. That dynamic could change if the Freedom Caucus wins control in 2026. 
The caucus may find itself on the defensive this campaign season after several of its members and allies were embroiled in a controversy, known as Checkgate, involving the delivery of campaign donations on the House floor, which is currently under criminal investigation. After a legislative committee determined the checks did not constitute bribery, the House unanimously voted to approve a report that said: “the conduct that occurred on the House floor was undesirable and must never occur again.” 
Seventeen of the Senate’s 31 districts will be on the ballot this year. To gain a majority in the upper chamber, the caucus needs to win at least 14 of those races to bolster the two Senators it endorsed in 2024 — Sens. Tim French, R-Cody, and Laura Pearson, R-Kemmerer. Neither is up for reelection this year. 
There are several other incumbents not up for reelection that the caucus can count on for votes, but their fidelity varies by issue. 
Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, and Troy McKeown, R-Gillette, for example, are largely ideologically aligned with the caucus but clashed with House leadership during negotiations over a property tax bill in 2025. Or, take Casper Republican Sen. Charles Scott, one of Wyoming’s most senior lawmakers. Scott supported caucus-backed legislation to significantly expand school choice in Wyoming in 2026. However, Scott is a self-described “pro-choice” lawmaker and regularly votes against bills to restrict or prohibit abortion. 
Sen. Charles Scott, R-Casper, seen during the 2025 Wyoming Legislature. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile) 
Meanwhile, at least five incumbent senators are not up for reelection who are neither caucus allies nor members. Those lawmakers include Sens. Jim Anderson, R-Casper; Ed Cooper, R-Ten Sleep; Barry Crago, R-Cheyenne; Gary Crum, R-Laramie, and Tara Nethercott, R-Cheyenne. 
As such, the Freedom Caucus is heading into the primary election at a slight disadvantage. Whether the group can win a majority in the Senate rests on a handful of races. 
The marquee competition among those is likely Speaker of the House Chip Neiman of Hulett versus the incumbent Sen. Ogden Driskill of Devils Towers. The two Republicans will square off in the primary election for Senate District 1, which encompasses the northeastern corner of the state, including all of Crook County and sections of Campbell and Weston counties. 
The two lawmakers embody the Republican split in the statehouse: Neiman belongs to the Freedom Caucus while Driskill represents the traditional wing of the Wyoming GOP. 
Like Neiman, Republican Reps. Abby Angelos of Gillette, Paul Hoeft of Powell, Ken Pendergraft of Sheridan and Daniel Singh of Cheyenne will attempt to make the leap from the House to the Senate. 
Pendergraft and Hoeft identify as members of the caucus, while Singh regularly votes alongside the bloc but left the group earlier this year. Angelos, meanwhile, does not identify as a member but also routinely votes with the caucus and crafted the caucus-backed budget as a member of the Joint Appropriations Committee. 
Singh will challenge Republican Sen. Evie Brennan, R-Cheyenne, for her seat in Laramie County. 

Rep. Ken Pendergraft, R-Sheridan, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheynne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)

Pendergraft is running for Senate District 21, an open seat in Sheridan County. Senate President Bo Biteman has represented the district since 2019 and is now running for U.S. House. Pendergraft will face Republican Melissa Butcher, a local business owner, in the primary election. 
Hoeft, a first-term representative, will compete against R.J. Kost, a former senator, in the Republican primary election for Senate District 19, which spans Big Horn and Park counties. Sen. Dan Laursen, R-Powell, is not running for reelection after representing the district since 2023. 
Angelos is running for Gillette’s Senate District 23 against Dwayne Dillinger, executive director of Campbell County Parks and Recreation. The two Republicans will vie for the seat currently held by Sen. Eric Barlow, who is running for governor.  
One win the caucus can likely count on will be in Senate District 3, where Sen. Cheri Steinmetz, R-Torrington, is running unopposed. She’s represented the district since 2019. 
Casper Republican Sen. Bob Ide, an ally of the caucus, will face a challenger after serving his first term in the upper chamber. Republican Lisa Engebretsen, a realtor, is challenging him for the Senate District 29 seat. 
Several incumbents, who are not aligned with the caucus, also face Republican challengers. That includes Sen. Taft Love, R-Cheyenne, who was appointed to Senate District 6 in September when Darin Smith vacated the seat to serve as the U.S. Attorney for Wyoming. Wheatland’s Roy Birt, who was nominated alongside Love to fill the vacancy, will challenge Taft in the Republican primary. Birt donated to Freedom Caucus members in 2024, according to campaign finance records, including Rep. Tomi Strock and Jeanette Ward, a former lawmaker seeking a rematch.
Sen. Cale Case, R-Lander, long a thorn in the side of the Freedom Caucus, will face challenger Lisa Wilson in the primary election. Sen. Wendy Schuler, R-Evanston, will face three Republican opponents — Jen Hegeman, Tina Johnson and Chris Katzl. 
The Senate’s two Democratic incumbents — Sens. Mike Gierau of Jackson and Chris Rothfuss of Laramie — are running unopposed.

title: Wyoming’s water future depends on holding corporate utilities accountable
description:
As water demands rise in the West, we must prioritize community input and take climate change seriously, writes guest columnist Emma Jones.
The post Wyoming’s water future depends on holding corporate utilities accountable appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
If you do any eavesdropping in Wyoming’s public spaces, you hear the same set of worries from people — what is the summer going to bring? Where are we going to get our water from? It’s a pretty rational set of concerns, especially considering that Wyoming just experienced its warmest winter and worst snowpack on record. 

Opinion

Wyomingites understand that water is not abstract. It sustains our communities, our ranches, our recreation economy and the landscapes that define this state. Yet at the same moment these concerns are growing, many of the most critical decisions affecting Wyoming’s water future are being driven by monopolistic utility companies and corporate interests with remarkably little public scrutiny.
In the last several months, federal officials at the Environmental Protection Agency have repeatedly signed off on efforts to delay coal ash cleanup at some of the most contaminated groundwater sites in the country — all while Rocky Mountain Power, Wyoming’s largest utility company, doubles down on an aging fleet of coal plants in the midst of a worsening climate crisis. On May 28, the EPA held a public hearing on yet another round of coal ash rollbacks, including plans to exempt hundreds of coal ash dumps from regulation and weaken safeguards designed to protect our water supply from contaminants, including arsenic, lithium and lead. You can submit an official public comment up until Friday at the EPA’s comment portal. Coal ash poses a direct and immediate threat to groundwater in Wyoming, but it’s only part of a bigger problem.
The unfortunate reality is that utility companies have enormous sway over our water resources — whether it’s the type of energy resources they prioritize, the developments they invest in or the downstream impacts of climate change. And if we want to protect our water, we need to start paying closer attention to what monopolistic utilities are doing.
Pressures on our water resources are likely to intensify as utilities pursue massive growth in electricity demand tied to data centers and industrial expansion. A couple of weeks ago, I listened in on Berkshire Hathaway’s annual shareholder meeting, where new CEO Greg Abel (formerly the head of Berkshire Hathaway Energy) enthusiastically endorsed data center development as a key opportunity for Berkshire-owned utility companies, including Rocky Mountain Power and its parent company, PacifiCorp. Yet, Wyoming policymakers have done little to establish guardrails around the scale, pace or water impacts of this development.
While community members are right to be concerned about the water usage of data centers themselves, a much bigger concern for me is the water consumption that accompanies the vast expansion of energy resources like natural gas.
Wyoming is at a crossroads — from climate to snowpack to the recent boom in data center development. These may seem like different issues, but the truth is that they are all connected. If we want to address water usage and the long-term health of the landscapes we all rely on, we need to prioritize real solutions:

We need to hold corporations, and especially private utility companies, to clear, enforceable and timely standards for reporting and remediating water contamination and usage.
We need to prioritize community input and ensure that communities across the state have the tools they need to effectively evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of development.
We need to start taking climate seriously. For utilities, that means prioritizing renewable energy resources and having a clear plan for an energy transition that puts communities first. It also means that state leaders should take water scarcity seriously when evaluating future energy development.

More than anything, we need a standard of honesty from the corporations that plan to operate in Wyoming, and we need officials who are willing to hold corporations to that standard.
Wyoming is at a crossroads, but we have the opportunity to advocate for what direction we go in. We can choose a future that prioritizes the sense of community that makes Wyoming a great place to live and that is sustainable for hardworking Wyomingites. We can work toward policies that allow us to grow while protecting our access to clean water and public lands. This fall, we can vote for representatives who prioritize honesty and accountability from corporate interests like Rocky Mountain Power.
I commented on the EPA’s latest round of coal ash rollbacks because protecting our groundwater is critical for Wyoming communities. But coal ash is only part of a much larger conversation about who gets to shape Wyoming’s future. The decisions utility companies make today — about coal plants, natural gas expansion, renewable energy and industrial growth — will shape Wyoming’s water future for decades. Wyoming cannot control the snowpack. But we can decide whether we allow short-term corporate interests to dictate the future of one of our most precious resources.

description: On Jan. 25, 1998, a 37-year old John Elway lined up on the 12-yard line at Qualcomm Stadium in San Diego. It was the third quarter of Super Bowl XXXII, and Elway’s Denver Broncos, tied 17-17 with the Green Bay Packers, needed a first down. Elway took the snap and dropped back, but he couldn’t […]
text:
John Elway of the Denver Broncos passes the ball to Terrell Davis during the Broncos' Super Bowl win over the Green Bay Packers on Jan. 25, 1998. (Photo by Lutz Bongarts/Bongarts/Getty Images)On Jan. 25, 1998, a 37-year old John Elway lined up on the 12-yard line at Qualcomm Stadium in San Diego. It was the third quarter of Super Bowl XXXII, and Elway’s Denver Broncos, tied 17-17 with the Green Bay Packers, needed a first down.
 


This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.



Elway took the snap and dropped back, but he couldn’t find an open receiver. So he dashed off to the right until he dove forward as he met three Packers defenders who sent him spinning in the air. It was a spectacular conclusion to a key play that’s come to be known as “The Helicopter.” Elway got the first down, and two plays later running back Terrell Davis, who was playing with a migraine, scored the go-ahead touchdown.
The Broncos, founded in 1960, had a rough early go as a pro team. The franchise didn’t have a winning season until 1973. But soon the team entered a decades-long era of success, endearing themselves to local fans and becoming the object of Colorado lore. The team made it to the Super Bowl for the first time in 1977, then three more times before the 1997 season, though it failed to capture the championship in each of those games.
A big reason for the team’s growing success was Elway, a college star who joined the roster in 1983. He led the Broncos to the Super Bowl after the 1986, 1987 and 1989 seasons. The team’s luck would turn around during Super Bowl XXXII in San Diego. After The Helicopter, the Broncos maintained their dominance over the Packers and won their first NFL championship. They’d go on to repeat the feat the following year, when they beat the Atlanta Falcons 31-19 in storybook fashion: Elway was voted the Super Bowl MVP, and it was the last professional football game he played.
The Broncos appeared in three more Super Bowls, winning one, for a total of eight. Only the New England Patriots have made it to more Super Bowls (11).
“The Denver Broncos have been one of pro football’s biggest winners since the merger of the American and National Football Leagues in 1970,” according to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. “The Broncos’ on-the-field success is more than matched by a spectacular attendance record of sellout crowds.”
For many years, those crowds gathered to watch their team at a site west of downtown Denver at first known as Bears Stadium, when it sat 35,000. The facility was later expanded and dubbed Mile High Stadium. The team’s current home opened in 2001, immediately south of the old site, as Invesco Field at Mile High, but that stadium is expected soon to be replaced. Future Broncos fans can plan to watch their home team play at a new stadium with a retractable roof at Burnham Yard, just southwest of downtown. The facility is scheduled to open in 2031.

text:
The U.S. Capitol on July 2, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Coloradans will vote in primary elections June 30 to determine which candidates will represent their party in the general election in November.

The elections cover Colorado’s four statewide constitutional offices, one U.S. Senate seat, all eight of the state’s congressional districts, state legislative districts and other races. Colorado Newsline sent questionnaires to candidates in contested primary races and is publishing responses as part of its voter guide to help Coloradans make informed choices.
Colorado’s 8th Congressional District is represented by Gabe Evans, a Fort Lupton Republican who is running for reelection with no primary challenger. Colorado state Rep. Manny Rutinel of Commerce City and former Colorado state Rep. Shannon Bird of Westminster are running in the Democratic primary, and whoever wins that race at the end of June will face Evans in November.
The 8th District, which includes the northern Denver suburbs and extends into Greeley, is Colorado’s most competitive district. It is also the state’s newest congressional district, drawn by an independent redistricting commission after the 2020 census.
Ballots were scheduled to be mailed to all registered voters in Colorado starting June 8.
Voters can contact their county clerk if they have not received their ballot or check the online BallotTrax system. They can also visit the secretary of state’s website to make a plan to vote in person ahead of or on Election Day. Ballots need to be received by the county clerk by 7 p.m. on that day, so voters should mail their ballot at least eight days ahead of time or drop it off in person.
Evan Munsing, a private equity consultant and Marine veteran, responded to Newsline’s questionnaire shortly before dropping out of the Democratic primary.
 Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, Democrats
 



Manny Rutinel
Age: 31
City of residence: Commerce City
Occupation: State representative
 


 



Shannon Bird
Age: 57
City of residence: Westminster
Occupation: Attorney, former state representative
 


What do residents in your district say is the biggest issue, and how will you work to address it?
RUTINEL: Residents tell me they’re worried about Donald Trump: his attacks on our democracy and his actions driving up the cost of living. For me, fighting Trump is personal. I was raised by a single immigrant mom, and I worked and studied hard to become an economist with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. As a Colorado legislator, I passed laws to fight Trump, protect our right to vote and stop ICE from terrorizing Latino families like mine. Now I’m running to bring that fight to Trump in Congress. Unfortunately, my opponent Shannon Bird was the only Democrat to vote with Republicans to allow police to cooperate with ICE, and let ICE raid our schools and hospitals. Trump is making life too expensive. I grew up on food stamps and Medicaid, the same programs Trump and Gabe Evans are destroying to give tax breaks to billionaires. His tariffs drive up the cost of groceries and housing. His budget forces millions of Americans off their healthcare. In Congress, I will lower costs, expand tax credits, make billionaires pay what they owe, and fight Trump’s reckless tariffs. I’ll deliver results that make life better and stop Trump’s cruelty and corruption.
BIRD: Everywhere I go, I hear from voters that the cost of healthcare is too high and that it’s getting worse. This issue is personal to me — I’ve been uninsured and know what it’s like to worry about not being able to go to the doctor. That’s why in the Colorado Legislature, I took on the big insurance companies to lower healthcare costs and expanded Medicaid. Unfortunately, both Gabe Evans and Manny Rutinel voted for steep Medicaid cuts — pushing healthcare out of reach for the one in three people in our district who rely on Medicaid. In Congress, I’ll fight with everything I’ve got to reverse the cuts to Medicaid and Medicare, and to restore healthcare subsidies for private insurance. I will also work to expand Medicare to cover vision, dental, and hearing, fight to lower the cost of prescription drugs, and to pass a public option to lower costs for everyone. 
What is your reaction to how Congress recently has stood by as President Donald Trump claimed powers that traditionally belonged to the legislative branch, such as those related to war, government spending and tariffs?
RUTINEL: It is a disgraceful abdication of Congress’s most basic constitutional duties. Trump imposed tariffs that raise prices on working families, poured billions of taxpayer dollars into the funding of masked ICE agents trained to terrorize our communities, and started wars without any plans, all while Congress does nothing. These are powers the Constitution gives to Congress, not the president. The current Republican majority has chosen to serve as rubber stamps for Trump’s cruelty and corruption instead of serving the people who elected them. Gabe Evans and his colleagues were elected to lower costs, not to hand their authority to a president who uses it to make life more expensive and worse for working families and seniors. In Congress, I will hold Trump and his administration accountable for their actions and fight to stop his abuses of power. That means using hearings and subpoenas to hold the Trump Administration accountable, and using the power of the purse to reassert Congress’s role. We need honest, accountable leadership that fights for working families and knows deep in their bones the struggles they face. I promise to always fight for those who have been left out, left behind, or left without a voice. 
BIRD: We’re all tired of seeing corrupt politicians in Washington stand by and do nothing as Donald Trump marches us into war and tanks our economy. In Congress, I won’t stand by — I’ll do what I’ve always done: fight for my constituents, defend our democratic values, and roll up my sleeves to deliver results. In contrast, Gabe Evans has aided and abetted the Trump administration at every turn. He has stood by and done nothing about the war in Iran that is causing gas prices to skyrocket, let Trump withhold federal funding from our district, and voted for the tariffs that have caused the cost of everything from groceries to housing to go up. In Congress, I will fight to repeal Trump’s tariffs on day one, reassert Congress’s authority over war powers, and work tirelessly to make life more affordable. We need a congresswoman who listens to us, not one who lets the president run roughshod and usurp checks and balances.
Describe your approach to citizen engagement, such as whether you will appear at in-person town hall meetings and answer unscreened questions from residents?
RUTINEL: I believe Democracy only works when it belongs to all of us, and that starts with showing up. As a state representative, I host regular town halls where constituents ask questions and provide feedback. I have shown up to in-person town halls in the 8th District because the people of this district deserve to be heard. Gabe Evans doesn’t hold public in-person town halls because he’s scared of his own constituents. That is unacceptable. In Congress, I will hold regular in-person town hall meetings across the district and take questions from anyone who shows up. I was a sponsor of Colorado’s Equal Access to Public Meetings Act because I believe all Coloradans deserve to participate in the discussions shaping their lives. I also support making voting records, committee hearings, and legislative debates easily accessible online. My campaign does not take corporate PAC money because I believe elected officials should answer to the people, not corporate special interests. My opponent, Shannon Bird, was one of the top recipients of corporate PAC donations during her time in the Legislature. The people of this district deserve a representative who works for them and looks them in the eye and answers their questions honestly. 
BIRD: A good leader shows up — and I’m proud to have held over 90 town halls and community coffees during my time in the Legislature, and will continue to do so in Congress. It is unconscionable that Gabe Evans has not held a single in-person town hall to answer for his votes. Across this campaign, I’ve made over 170 stops across the district, meeting with small businesses, healthcare providers, farmers, and community institutions, so I can learn about the issues that matter most and be ready to hit the ground running on day one. I have also shown up at places Democratic leaders don’t normally show up by holding a series of “Brews with Bird” events that are open to the public and provide voters an opportunity to ask candid questions and participate in unscripted conversations with me. Additionally, I have personally called thousands of voters to learn about the issues that matter most. I will continue to be accessible, transparent, and meet voters where they are when in Congress, where my focus will be to serve the people of Colorado’s 8th District.
How will you respond to Trump administration actions, such as the withholding of federal disaster assistance, that appear to punish Colorado over political disagreements?
RUTINEL: Trump is using federal funding as a political weapon against Colorado, and it is hitting the working families of this district hard. The Trump administration has targeted over $275 million in federal funding intended to support the 8th District alone. About one in four people in our district rely on Medicaid for health insurance, and Trump’s budget would siphon over $625 billion from Medicaid over the next 10 years. His administration has even threatened to withhold SNAP funding that families depend on to feed hungry children. The Coloradans paying the price are working families, seniors, children, and people with disabilities who did nothing wrong. A disaster is a disaster, and hungry families are hungry families, regardless of how their state voted. In Congress, I will fight to ensure that federal funding is based on need, not on politics and corruption. I will push for transparency and accountability so no president can weaponize federal dollars against states that disagree with him. I will use every tool available, including oversight hearings, lawsuits, legislation, and the power of the purse, to protect Colorado from this kind of retribution. When Trump tries to punish Coloradans, we need leaders in Congress who won’t back down. 
BIRD: Coloradans expect our federal tax dollars to come home, but Gabe Evans has stood by and done nothing as Trump withholds federal funding from our district — whether that be federal disaster assistance, education funding, or transportation grants — for his own political grudges. I’m proud to be the only candidate in this race who has taken on Trump already. In the Colorado Legislature, I passed the law that provided funding for our state’s attorney general to sue the Trump administration, which he has successfully done over withheld funding. In Congress, I’ll always work to bring our money home and stand up to the Trump administration when they withhold funding, including working to pass legislation to secure funding for our district, conducting oversight, and holding the president accountable to ensure that our state isn’t punished.
What, if anything, must Congress do to ensure the security of elections?
RUTINEL: Congress must protect every American’s right to vote and ensure that our elections are free, fair, and secure. These issues are not new to me. In the state House, I’ve sponsored and passed bills to expand voting rights and fight back against Trump’s attacks on our democracy. Congress should pass legislation that protects voters from suppression, ensures adequate funding for election security infrastructure, and prevents political interference in how votes are counted and certified. We need to reverse Citizens United and get dark money out of politics because special interests and dark money groups try to buy our elections. We need to give that power back to the people. I also believe we should explore voting reforms that give power back to the will of working people. Congress should consider restricting firearms near polling locations, as Colorado has already done, to make sure every voter can cast their ballot without intimidation. We should also prevent masked ICE agents from trying to intimidate Americans at polling locations. Elections belong to the people, and I will fight to keep it that way.
BIRD: The right to vote is sacred. Here in Colorado, we’re proud to lead the country in voter protection, efforts I’ve supported in the Legislature. On day one in Congress, I will co-sponsor the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act to protect voting rights across the country, and will also support the Freedom to Vote Act to make Election Day a federal holiday, expand voting registration and access, and make our elections systems more secure. I’ll also work to ban partisan gerrymandering nationwide and stand up to Trump and Republicans, who are working to make voting harder.

Colorado’s 5th Congressional District is represented by Jeff Crank, a Colorado Springs Republican who is running for reelection with no primary challenger. Jessica Killin and Joe Reagan are running in the Democratic primary, and whoever wins that race at the end of June will face Crank in November.
The 5th District is centered on Colorado Springs and leans Republican.

 Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, Democrats
 



Jessica Killin
Age: 52
City of residence: Colorado Springs
Occupation: Public servant
 


 



Joe Reagan
Age: 44
City of residence: Colorado Springs
Occupation: Nonprofit director
 


What do residents in your district say is the biggest issue, and how will you work to address it?
KILLIN: We have an affordability crisis here in El Paso County. Families are struggling to afford housing, healthcare, childcare, and groceries. As gas prices continue to skyrocket because of the Iran conflict, families are being squeezed even further. First, I would end the illegal tariffs that are raising prices for hardworking Coloradans. Jeff Crank has repeatedly voted to protect these harmful tariffs. I would work to lower our housing costs by increasing housing supply in the Pikes Peak region and improving access for first-time homebuyers. I would also collaborate with federal, state, and local partners to increase the availability of affordable, quality childcare. Finally, I would work long-term to build out a more robust middle class through a fairer and equitable tax and economic policy so that Coloradans have the opportunity to live their American Dream. 
REAGAN: The biggest issue I hear about across the district is affordability — the growing sense that working families are being priced out of the American dream. Whether it’s housing, healthcare, groceries, insurance premiums, or childcare, too many Coloradans feel like they’re working harder while falling further behind. Housing is a major part of that challenge. We need to increase supply at every level, especially for first-time homebuyers and working families, supporting communities as they build workforce and entry-level housing while ensuring ordinary families aren’t forced to compete against massive institutional investors buying up single-family homes. We also have to address the broader pressures driving costs higher. Wildfire risk and rising insurance premiums are squeezing families across Colorado. Healthcare costs continue to outpace wage growth. AI and new technologies are rapidly changing the workforce, and we need to invest in education, apprenticeships, and workforce development so workers aren’t left behind. Affordability and democracy are deeply connected. People are frustrated because the system responds more quickly to corporate lobbyists and political donors than to working families. I support reforms that increase transparency, strengthen competition, and ensure Congress is focused on lowering costs and creating opportunity — not protecting special interests.
What is your reaction to how Congress recently has stood by as President Donald Trump claimed powers that traditionally belonged to the legislative branch, such as those related to war, government spending and tariffs?
KILLIN: El Paso County needs a representative who is willing to stand up to leaders from either party. With Jeff Crank’s blessing, Trump has continuously hurt Southern Colorado – cutting childcare funding, moving Space Command, and vetoing a bill for safe drinking water for Colorado. I will always put the people of the Pikes Peak Region over partisan games. Jeff Crank has also allowed the illegal conflict in Iran that is costing tens of billions in taxpayer dollars and sacrificing American lives, which is making life even more expensive here at home. We need a leader who will fight for Colorado and work to take back the power of Congress, rather than do as they’re told by their party bosses.
REAGAN: Congress has increasingly ceded powers to the executive branch for years, regardless of which party controls the White House — and that trend has weakened democratic accountability and the constitutional balance our system depends on. We’re seeing the consequences now on tariffs, war powers, and federal spending. The administration’s tariff policies function as a tax on working families and small businesses, raising costs while making it harder for local businesses to compete against massive corporations with larger supply chains and pricing power. I’ve heard from small business owners across El Paso County who are struggling with the resulting uncertainty. As a combat veteran, I believe Congress has a responsibility to fully debate and authorize military action rather than allowing administrations to expand conflicts without oversight. I served during the Global War on Terror and saw firsthand the long-term impact these decisions have on service members, veterans, and military families. Too often, working-class Americans bear the burden of wars while well-connected interests profit from them. Congress must restore constitutional guardrails — reclaim authority over trade and war powers, strengthen oversight, and rebuild public trust. Americans deserve confidence that decisions are made in the public interest, not to benefit political donors or insider networks.
Describe your approach to citizen engagement, such as whether you will appear at in-person town hall meetings and answer unscreened questions from residents?

I commit to hosting in-person town halls at least once every quarter, answering unscreened questions, and consistently meeting with all constituents, including those who disagree with me. This community deserves real, responsive leadership. That is the job of a member of the House of Representatives.
REAGAN: Representation starts with accessibility and presence. I’ve tried to run a campaign consistent with how I would serve in Congress: showing up in person, engaging directly with residents, and lowering barriers to participation rather than creating them. I strongly support holding regular in-person town halls with unscreened questions. But engagement should go beyond traditional town halls. Not everyone can attend an evening event, so I want to combine in-person meetings with virtual forums and transparent digital communication to ensure people across the district can participate. Congress also needs to rethink constituent correspondence. People deserve to know their concerns are being heard. I would work to provide more timely, transparent responses and regularly communicate about what we’re hearing from the community. I’m active in local nonprofits and community organizations, and this year I’ll serve as president of the Colorado Springs Rotary Club. Those connections matter because public service shouldn’t isolate representatives from everyday life in their district. For too long, people here have felt disconnected from their representatives. I want constituents to see me regularly in the community — not just during election season.
How will you respond to Trump administration actions, such as the withholding of federal disaster assistance, that appear to punish Colorado over political disagreements?
KILLIN: I will fight like hell for Colorado. I’m not afraid of President Trump, and when he tries to retaliate against our state, I will be unrelenting in holding him accountable and pushing back. I will also build relationships and work across the aisle to form a unified voice to protect Coloradans. It’s unacceptable to withhold federal disaster assistance or make critical national security decisions — like the location of Space Command — based on petty political fights. I will lead with integrity and always put the people of El Paso County first. 
REAGAN: I believe it is deeply inappropriate for disaster relief, economic development assistance, or federal support programs to be influenced by political disagreements or election results. The federal government is supposed to serve all Americans equally, regardless of party affiliation or how a state voted in the last election. We’ve seen growing concerns not only around disaster assistance, but also around uncertainty affecting programs that local communities and small businesses rely on, including support connected to Small Business Development Centers. When federal agencies appear to treat states differently based on politics, it undermines public trust and hurts communities that depend on those resources. In Colorado, disaster assistance is not an abstract issue. Wildfires, drought, severe weather, and rising insurance costs are already placing enormous pressure on families, small businesses, and local governments. Federal support should be based on need, transparency, and objective standards — not partisan considerations. Congress has an important oversight responsibility here. I believe lawmakers must hold agency leaders and administrations accountable to ensure federal programs are distributed fairly, consistently, and in accordance with the law. I have full confidence in Colorado’s election officials and the integrity of our state’s election system. At the federal level, Congress should focus on protecting both election security and public confidence in democratic participation. That includes strengthening cybersecurity support for states, protecting election workers from threats and intimidation, and ensuring states have the resources necessary to administer elections fairly and efficiently. The SAVE Act is a prime example of legislation that gets this backward, imposing burdensome documentary proof-of-citizenship requirements that would disenfranchise millions of eligible American voters while solving a problem that does not meaningfully exist. It is a solution in search of a problem, and I oppose it. Congress must also address partisan gerrymandering. Politicians should not be choosing their voters. Colorado’s independent redistricting system is a better model. Congress should strengthen protections under the Voting Rights Act and ensure every eligible voter can participate freely and safely. No American should feel intimidated or discouraged from voting. Secure elections and accessible elections are not competing goals. A healthy democracy requires both.

The U.S. Capitol on July 2, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Coloradans will vote in primary elections June 30 to determine which candidates will represent their party in the general election in November.

The elections cover Colorado’s four statewide constitutional offices, one U.S. Senate seat, all eight of the state’s congressional districts, state legislative districts and other races. Colorado Newsline sent questionnaires to candidates in contested primary races and is publishing responses as part of its voter guide to help Coloradans make informed choices.
Colorado’s 4th Congressional District is represented by Lauren Boebert, a Windsor Republican who is running for reelection with no primary challenger. Retired Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official Eileen Laubacher will be the sole Democrat on the June primary ballot, but clinical psychologist Jenna Preston is running as a write-in candidate. Whoever wins that race at the end of June will face Boebert in November.
Since launching her campaign last year, Laubacher has established a substantial fundraising advantage over her rivals, raising more money than every other candidate of either party in the race combined.
The 4th District, which includes the Eastern Plains and most of Douglas County, is Colorado’s most conservative district.
Ballots were scheduled to be mailed to all registered voters in Colorado starting June 8.
Voters can contact their county clerk if they have not received their ballot or check the online BallotTrax system. They can also visit the secretary of state’s website to make a plan to vote in person ahead of or on Election Day. Ballots need to be received by the county clerk by 7 p.m. on that day, so voters should mail their ballot at least eight days ahead of time or drop it off in person.
Trisha Calvarese, who was Boebert’s Democratic opponent in 2024, dropped out of the race this year after she brought a lawsuit that attempted but failed to challenge Laubacher’s eligibility to run as a Democrat.
 Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, Democrats
 



Eileen Laubacher
Age: 57
City of residence: Highlands Ranch
Occupation: Retired Navy rear admiral
 


 



Jenna Preston (write-in)
Age: 54
City of residence: Parker
Occupation: Licensed clinical psychologist
 


What do residents in your district say is the biggest issue, and how will you work to address it?
LAUBACHER: I hear most about costs. The price of gas, groceries, healthcare, insurance — all skyrocketing. Families are struggling. Our representatives have a responsibility to act immediately and provide relief to working families. Lauren Boebert has repeatedly refused to do so. She has voted for tariffs, voted to cut healthcare funding, and acted as a roadblock to needed infrastructure funding. Boebert has the power to help working people. Instead, she acts as an obstacle to lowering costs. No one should have to worry about how they will put food on the table or access medicine. My only job in office will be to fight on behalf of the people and communities of Colorado — to ensure that no one is being left behind. 
PRESTON: Trust. Residents in our district have lost trust in those elected to represent them, to be honest, understand, show up, or follow through on promises. Our current congresswoman jeopardizes our healthcare and my Democratic opponent has not been honest about her voting record and not living in the district. Americans are losing trust in the news, social media, our justice system, and neighbors with different political views. Americans worry they will not have access to healthcare, social security, decisions about their own bodies, who they can marry, their ability to pay their bills, or see their children own a home someday. Residents see waste and corruption across the government while politicians on both sides get wealthy. They fear losing programs that support rural communities, veterans, women’s health, public education, small businesses, and healthcare. The arrival of AI has only deepened uncertainty and distrust. As a therapist for the past 30 years, I understand the importance of establishing and maintaining trust. I chose a career built on listening, understanding people’s struggles and what keeps them up at night, and helping create a path forward. I would do the same in Congress. 
What is your reaction to how Congress recently has stood by as President Donald Trump claimed powers that traditionally belonged to the legislative branch, such as those related to war, government spending and tariffs?
LAUBACHER: The Iran War is bad policy — one that Lauren Boebert cast the deciding vote to continue. We are spending tens of billions of dollars abroad and risking American lives just to raise gas prices and make it harder for people to get by. She has also repeatedly backed the tariffs that resulted in nothing but rising costs. This is not what Colorado’s 4th District wants. Our communities are being harmed by Boebert’s continued support of bad policy. All we are asking is for her to take responsibility and do her job, and she is clearly not up to the task.
PRESTON: President Donald Trump is one person, but he operates within a system that has condoned and perpetuated his abuse of power. When institutions fail to enforce accountability, power shifts away from the people and toward one individual. That is dangerous in any system, whether in families, schools, workplaces, or the government. Sometimes this happens out of fear or powerlessness, but in this case due to weakness, complacency, and corruption. Congress has become deeply divided and ineffective, failing to work together to protect the constitutional authority of the legislative branch outlined in Article I of the Constitution. Instead of serving as a co-equal branch of government, Congress has stood by while our president, narcissistic authoritarian tendencies makes unchecked decisions involving war, tariffs, and federal spending. This weakens democratic checks and balances and harms public trust in government. As a therapist, I have learned that progress only happens when people are willing to listen, collaborate, and work through conflict instead of deepening division. I never ask my patients, “Who did you vote for?” I ask, “How can I help?” We need leaders who can work across political differences, defend democratic institutions, and focus on improving the lives of everyday Americans.
Describe your approach to citizen engagement, such as whether you will appear at in-person town hall meetings and answer unscreened questions from residents?
LAUBACHER: The work does not end on the campaign trail. I will commit to holding regular town halls and meet people where they are. I know that people are tired of representatives who have been in D.C. for too many years and have forgotten their needs. It’s the reason we have politicians like Lauren Boebert making life more expensive and voting to hurt veterans, farmers, ranchers, and our communities. I promise to never stop meeting people face-to-face and answering their toughest questions.  
PRESTON: I chose a career as a therapist because it centers on in-person engagement. I have had the honor of sitting across from people, earning their trust, listening to their concerns, and working collaboratively to help create a path forward. In many ways, I have trained my whole life for this moment. I welcome difficult, unscreened questions because honest conversations are how trust is built. Our current congresswoman, Lauren Boebert, has not held a single in-person town hall in the 4th District. Instead, she has relied on scripted, audio-only town halls while continuing to support policies that would take healthcare away from many of the people she represents. I look forward to holding regular in-person town halls across our district, quarterly at a minimum and monthly when needed. I would also offer hybrid options so residents could participate by phone or video. In every setting, I would welcome unscreened questions from constituents. Serving this district means being present in the community. I will continue attending local potlucks, festivals, community meetings, and partnering with organizations like CSU Extension to stay connected to the people I serve. I want my local and Washington offices to feel welcoming and accessible to every constituent.
How will you respond to Trump administration actions, such as the withholding of federal disaster assistance, that appear to punish Colorado over political disagreements?
LAUBACHER: I’ll always push back on Washington every time out-of-touch politicians hurt our communities. I am not afraid to stand up to anyone who is hurting the people I represent, and I have no interest in appeasing partisan agendas or powerful interests. Lauren Boebert seems content to stand by as her constituents are punished for Washington squabbles. Service has been central to my life in the military and my life on the campaign trail — that will continue as an elected official. I am only concerned with the needs of the people I seek to represent, and I refuse to let politicians punish them over political games.
PRESTON: I have seen firsthand how federal assistance programs save lives and strengthen communities. I grew up in a flood zone in a small town in New Jersey, where my family depended on organizations like FEMA and the American Red Cross after devastating floods. I remember sorting through water-soaked possessions, while federal aid helped my single mother rebuild our home where she raised three daughters. As a therapist in community mental health clinics, I worked with adults, children, and families who relied on federally funded Medicaid services to access care. As a clinical psychologist, I have treated military members coping with trauma from responding to hurricanes, floods, and wildfires across the country. I also have a sister who depends on Affordable Care Act funding for healthcare coverage. Federal disaster assistance and public support programs are not political favors, they are lifelines for Americans in moments of crisis. Any administration that withholds aid to punish states over political disagreements is abandoning its responsibility to serve the American people. In Congress, I will fight to protect these essential programs and ensure that compassion, fairness, and public service, not political retaliation, guide federal decisions. Who better than a psychologist to guide us through crises.
What, if anything, must Congress do to ensure the security of elections?
LAUBACHER: We must always ensure that American elections are safe and secure, and Colorado has worked hard to do that. We also have real threats to our elections coming from overseas actors like China or Russia — Congress needs to take those threats seriously. This is not a partisan issue. Every American deserves to be heard. I fought to ensure that American Democracy remains strong, and to see representatives like Lauren Boebert challenge that value, and actively work to undermine it, is shameful. Congress can’t give credence to baseless challenges to our electoral system, because that makes things harder for every American regardless of political affiliation or partisanship.
PRESTON: Congress must protect the integrity, accessibility, and public trust of our elections and re-assuring Americans that our elections are secure and remain a model for the world. I have voted by mail since 2003, when I moved overseas with my husband during his Air Force service. For more than two decades, I have relied on mail voting without ever questioning the security of my ballot. At the same time, Congress must address the influence of money in politics starting with overturning the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision and reducing the power of super PACs and dark money in our democratic process. We need to inspire more participation in elections by making elections easier to understand and more accessible to voters, including reevaluating systems like caucus and assembly processes that involve only a small percentage of voters, like this 4th District race. Finally, we need to make it easier for everyday working Americans to run for office. Our democracy works best when elected leaders reflect the experiences and struggles of the people they serve — not only those with wealth, influence, or political connections. As a write-in candidate for Congress in Colorado’s 4th District, I would be honored to earn your vote.
